key_points: Mandatory license conditions must relate to project effects

quotes.text: by inserting “and are reasonably related to the effects of the project” after “of such reservation”.
quotes.why: Mandatory license conditions must relate to the project's effects.

2232.vs_current_law: The department that manages a federal reservation, including Interior for Indian reservations, can impose any condition it deems necessary to protect the reservation and its use.

2233.plain: Bars FERC from requiring license amendments for routine hydropower maintenance, repair or replacement, or for temporary operating variances caused by events outside the licensee's control. FERC must propose a rule within 90 days and finish within a further 180 days defining which alterations are substantial enough to need approval. Dam safety authority is preserved.
key_points: No FERC approval needed for routine hydropower maintenance

quotes.text: The Commission shall not require approval or an amendment to a project license for any routine maintenance, repair, or replacement of any portion of a project works
quotes.why: Routine dam maintenance no longer needs FERC sign-off.

2233.vs_current_law: FERC reviews many post-licensing changes individually. It opened an inquiry in November 2025 (Docket RM26-3).

2234.plain: Creates an expedited FERC license of 10 to 20 years for micro hydrokinetic projects of 5 megawatts or less (wave, tidal, current and free-flowing river turbines with no impoundment), with final action within 1 year of the application and categorical exclusions for low-disturbance activities.
key_points: One-year licensing for hydrokinetic projects up to 5 MW

quotes.text: The Commission shall take final action on an application for a license under this section not later than 1 year after the date on which the application is filed
quotes.why: A one-year license decision for small hydrokinetic projects.

2234.vs_current_law: Such projects use the general licensing or pilot project processes.

2241.plain: Widens FERC's special pay authority to economic and legal positions and strikes paragraph (6) of the same subsection.
key_points: FERC can use special pay rates for economists and lawyers

quotes.text: by striking “or mathematical” and inserting “mathematical, economic, or legal”
quotes.why: Adds economists and lawyers to FERC's special hiring authority.

2241.vs_current_law: The authority covers scientific, technological, engineering and mathematical positions, and the FERC Chairman must consult the Office of Personnel Management when setting pay.

2242.plain: Amends the cap on Bonneville's funding of the Northwest Power and Conservation Council, section 4(c)(10)(B) of the Northwest Power Act, by adding the words 'since the date of enactment' of this bill.
key_points: Technical change to the funding cap for the Northwest Power and Conservation Council

quotes.text: since the date of enactment of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026
quotes.why: The words added to the Council's funding cap.

2242.vs_current_law: Bonneville may fund the Council up to 0.10 mill for each kilowatt-hour of firm power it forecasts selling that year.

2243.plain: Lets FERC authorize its employees to perform law enforcement duties to protect the Chairman and Commissioners.
key_points: Protective detail authority for FERC commissioners

quotes.text: to perform law enforcement duties as needed to ensure the safety of the Chairman and Commissioners of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
quotes.why: Security for FERC commissioners.

2251.plain: Amends the offshore renewable energy section of the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act. Interior's duty changes from 'prevention of interference with reasonable uses' of the ocean to 'prevention of unreasonable interference with other uses'. Interior, in consultation with the Secretary of Commerce, may grant rights-of-way for electric transmission through national marine sanctuaries, with sanctuary permits lasting as long as the right-of-way. The Inflation Reduction Act's link between offshore wind leasing and oil and gas lease sales is preserved.
key_points: Offshore wind standard changes to 'unreasonable interference'
Transmission cables allowed through marine sanctuaries

quotes.text: by striking “prevention of interference with reasonable uses” and inserting “prevention of unreasonable interference with other uses”
quotes.why: The offshore wind test becomes 'unreasonable interference' with other uses.

2251.vs_current_law: Section 8(p)(4)(I) requires prevention of interference with reasonable uses of the exclusive economic zone, the high seas and the territorial seas.
2251.vs_epra_2024: The three Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act amendments come from EPRA 2024 (sec. 302(d)), with one change: sanctuary rights-of-way are no longer limited to electricity from renewable energy. EPRA's mandates do not appear here: one offshore oil and gas lease sale and one offshore wind lease sale a year from 2025 to 2029, 400,000 acres of wind leasing a year, and a 30-gigawatt offshore wind goal.

2252.plain: Directs Interior and Energy to identify preferred routes for offshore transmission cables within 2 years and review them every 3 years, makes Interior the lead agency for offshore transmission permitting, requires a final rule within 2 years, and lets Interior issue offshore transmission rights-of-way competitively or noncompetitively.
key_points: Planned offshore transmission routes within 2 years
Interior is lead agency; rights-of-way can be noncompetitive

quotes.text: shall identify preferred routes on the outer Continental Shelf for transmission cables and sub-seabed infrastructure
quotes.why: Interior and Energy must identify preferred offshore cable routes.

2252.vs_current_law: Each offshore transmission line is permitted on its own.
2252.vs_epra_2024: Not in EPRA 2024, which made offshore lines eligible for FERC backstop siting and cost allocation (kept in section 2101).

2301.plain:
Rewrites section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act. An 'adverse effect' must be reasonably foreseeable and must directly alter a historic property. Temporary alterations are excluded. Visual, atmospheric and audible effects are excluded unless they directly and significantly diminish the property. An 'undertaking' excludes projects whose only federal tie is a loan, guarantee or grant, the non-federal parts of a project, minor repairs, permit renewals and post-approval operations.

The process gets deadlines: 30 days to decide whether a project is an undertaking, 60 days for the agency's report, 90 days for a determination, then 60 days of consultation, 45 days for Advisory Council comments and 30 days for a final decision. Consultation must be finished by the time the NEPA document is completed, unless the Secretary grants an extension for extraordinary circumstances. State and tribal preservation officers who do not respond in 30 days are passed over, and the agency may decide in its sole discretion that other considerations outweigh preservation.

Courts give substantial deference and may only remand without vacatur or injunction; a preliminary injunction is available only for a likely violation of another law. Claims go to the courts of appeals, within 150 days, from parties who commented and suffered direct harm. A suit over a missed consultation deadline goes to a court where the project is located. Non-signatories cannot challenge programmatic agreements. State and tribal programs are evaluated every 2 years and lose grants if they miss consultation timelines.
key_points: Adverse effect limited to direct physical alteration; visual and noise effects mostly excluded
Loans and grants alone no longer trigger section 106
End-to-end deadlines; silence from a preservation officer after 30 days lets the agency proceed
Agency may find other considerations outweigh preservation 'in the sole discretion' of the official
150-day limit, court of appeals jurisdiction, remand without vacatur
Later National Register listings do not reopen a review

quotes.text: any visual, atmospheric, or audible element, unless the visual, atmospheric, or audible element would have a direct impact on a historic property that would significantly diminish the eligible characteristics of the historic property
quotes.why: Visual, atmospheric and audible effects mostly no longer count as adverse.

quotes.text: in the sole discretion of the Federal official and as otherwise allowed by law, other considerations outweigh the consideration of historic preservation as to any or all adverse effects of the undertaking
quotes.why: The agency may decide that other considerations outweigh preservation.

quotes.text: the only remedy the court may order is to remand, without vacatur or issuance of an injunction, the applicable agency action to the Federal agency
quotes.why: Remand is the only remedy, as in the NEPA title.

2301.vs_current_law: Section 106 is one sentence requiring agencies to 'take into account' effects on historic properties; the process lives in Advisory Council regulations (36 CFR part 800) with no statutory deadlines, a broad definition of adverse effect that includes visual and audible intrusions, and ordinary APA review.
2301.vs_epra_2024: Not in EPRA 2024. This is the first major permitting bill to rewrite section 106.

2302.plain: Authorizes $200 million a year for deposit in the Historic Preservation Fund for fiscal years 2027 through 2036. Deposits become available the next fiscal year without a further appropriation. Creates a $20 million-a-year grant program (fiscal years 2027 through 2030) for tribal historic preservation officers to build online databases of records and of properties of traditional religious or cultural importance, with protections against disclosing sensitive site locations.
key_points: $200 million a year for the Historic Preservation Fund through 2036
$20 million a year for tribal preservation databases

quotes.text: There is authorized to be appropriated for deposit in the Historic Preservation Fund $200,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2027 through 2036.
quotes.why: $200 million a year for the Historic Preservation Fund.

2302.vs_current_law: The fund was authorized at $150 million a year through fiscal year 2023 and has been awaiting reauthorization.
